stories.headline: Two pedestrians killed in crash on southbound I-25 on-ramp at Sixth Avenue in Denver
stories.summary:
Two pedestrians died in a late-night crash on the southbound Interstate 25 on-ramp at Sixth Avenue in Denver on Wednesday, according to the Denver Police Department. Police first posted about the fatal crash at 11:22 p.m. Wednesday.

An unidentified driver struck the two pedestrians on the ramp, and both died, police said in a 9:45 a.m. Thursday update. The Denver Office of the Medical Examiner will identify the victims. Information about the events leading up to the crash was not immediately available.

The interchange sits on the edge of Denver's Baker, Lincoln Park, Sun Valley and Valverde neighborhoods. The investigation is ongoing, and police have not said whether the driver remained at the scene or faces any charges.

stories.headline: CSU President Amy Parsons to step down at end of the year
stories.summary:
Colorado State University President Amy Parsons announced this week that she will resign effective Dec. 31, according to a letter to the campus community. Parsons became president in 2023 after more than a decade as the university's legal counsel and in other leadership roles. She did not specify why she is leaving, and said she and her husband will remain in Fort Collins.

CSU Chancellor Tony Frank said Rick Miranda, the longtime provost who has served as interim president before, will step in as interim president at the beginning of next year. Frank also confirmed that Rico Munn, executive vice chancellor, will succeed him after his July 1 retirement and will lead the search for the university's 17th president. That process will begin this spring and include campus engagement.

The president of CSU's faculty union chapter, Anders Fremstad, said the union is concerned about the sudden resignation and demanded a transparent search. He cited earlier unexplained departures, including former president Joyce McConnell and former provost Marion Underwood, and the cost of settlements with ex-administrators.

stories.headline: DOJ monitors decline Colorado's conditions, will not enter Adams County voting centers
stories.summary:
Federal Department of Justice election monitors will not enter voting centers in Adams County after declining restrictions Colorado placed on their access, state and local officials told Denver7. Secretary of State Jena Griswold said her office offered access under specific conditions, with her observers accompanying the monitors at all times.

The restrictions limited the monitors to speaking with a presiding election official about accessible voting equipment and bilingual poll workers, and to checking whether election materials were posted in Spanish. Griswold said a new state law requires DOJ monitors to be approved by her office before entering a voting center. Because the DOJ declined the terms, the monitors will be treated like any member of the public and have said they would stand 100 feet outside.

Adams County Clerk and Recorder Josh Zygielbaum said the secretary of state had approved the scope of access the observers requested, and that he was surprised to learn the DOJ decided not to accept it.

stories.headline: Colorado Republicans face question of relevance in legislative elections
stories.summary:
Tuesday's state legislative races will determine whether Colorado Republicans retain meaningful influence or are pushed further into the minority. Legislative contests have drawn more than $21 million in outside spending, much of it from conservative groups trying to blunt a potential Democratic wave.

Democrats, who have controlled state government since 2019, are one seat shy in each chamber of a two-thirds supermajority. They hold 43 of 65 House seats and 23 of 35 Senate seats. State Sen. John Carson, a Highlands Ranch Republican whose reelection may decide whether Democrats cross the threshold, warned of near one-party rule.

A supermajority would not change which party controls the legislature, but it would limit Republicans' ability to stop veto overrides, block rule changes, or prevent constitutional amendments from being referred to voters. Republican-aligned committees have outspent Democratic-aligned groups so far, with about $14 million spent to support Republicans.

stories.headline: Ethics complaint targets Denver mayor's chief strategist over law firm selection
stories.summary:
An anonymous Denver city employee has filed an ethics complaint accusing Mayor Mike Johnston's chief strategist, Jeff Dolan, of a potential conflict of interest in the city's selection of a law firm. The firm, Wheeler Trigg O'Donnell, was hired to defend Denver in a lawsuit brought by Everett Martinez, the former top lawyer at Denver International Airport, in which Dolan is a named defendant.

The Sept. 20 complaint, obtained by CBS Colorado through an open records request, asks the Board of Ethics to determine whether Dolan's participation on the selection panel constituted official action on a matter in which he had a substantial personal interest. It is the second Johnston cabinet member to face an ethics complaint over the selection. The complainant also criticized the contract's cost.

Mayor's office spokesperson Jon Ewing said the contract was done by the book and approved by Council, noting the city has used the firm for nearly two decades. He added that a complaint does not mean a violation occurred.

stories.headline: New Nordstrom Rack opens in Denver West area of Lakewood
stories.summary:
Nordstrom Rack opened two new Colorado stores this week, one in the Denver West area of Lakewood and another in Dillon. The Lakewood store is a 24,000-square-foot location at Denver West Village, north of Colorado Mills Shopping Center across West Colfax Avenue.

The Denver area already has six Nordstrom Racks, but observers said this store shows a stepped-up presentation, with new fixtures and merchandise not yet available at older stores. The store is paired with Whole Foods and Barnes & Noble in the plaza.

Senior vice president Cheri Botiz said the concept offers discounts of up to 70% on upscale brands. There are about 300 Rack stores nationally, and the openings come as holiday shopping expectations run high.

stories.headline: Denver software company Harper hires new CEO from Akamai as co-founder steps down
stories.summary:
Harper, a nine-year-old Denver software company, has hired a new chief executive from Akamai as its co-founder steps down, according to the Denver Business Journal.

The company more than doubled its workforce in 2025. The leadership change marks a new phase for the Denver-based developer.

Further details on the transition were not available in the excerpt of the report.

stories.headline: Teacher's rare T. rex footprint discovery goes on display at Denver museum
stories.summary:
A Colorado high school science teacher's discovery of dinosaur footprints during an expedition in North Dakota has led to a first-of-its-kind exhibit at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science.

Part of the trackway will go on public display at the museum on Friday, Oct. 30.

The exhibit highlights a rare T. rex find made by a teacher from Colorado.

stories.headline: Sunny, mild Thursday in Denver before rain returns Sunday night
stories.summary:
The National Weather Service in Boulder forecast sunshine and clear skies in Denver on Thursday, with a high of 64 degrees, about 4 degrees above the Oct. 29 average. Afternoon winds were expected to be calm at 5 to 8 mph, with clouds increasing in the evening and a low near 42.

For Halloween weekend, temperatures after dark are expected to sit in the 40s on the plains and fall to the 20s and 30s in the mountains and high valleys. Conditions should be mostly dry, aside from a 20 to 30% chance of snow showers in the mountains.

Saturday should be mostly sunny with some increased clouds for trick-or-treating. Rain is expected to return Sunday evening into Monday morning, with temperatures dipping into the low to mid 50s.

topStory.headline: Justice Department Says Democrats Misled Court in Alaska Senate Race Lawsuit, Files Amended Complaint
topStory.summary:
The Department of Justice on Thursday escalated its lawsuit over potential certification of Alaska's Senate election result, filing an amended complaint in federal court in Anchorage. The suit argues the outcome could be tainted by the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, a man who shares a name with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The amended filing adds a new legal claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution and incorporates details from a New York Times article published Wednesday.

The Times report described alleged efforts by people in the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola to recruit a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan into the race. The DOJ's amended complaint says Peltola's campaign, Alaskans For Mary, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee were aware of the purpose of his candidacy and "orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected." It also suggests the two groups misled U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason by stating in recent court filings that they lacked knowledge about why the retiree entered the race. Separately, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy late Wednesday ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment violated criminal or civil laws, citing the Times report.

In a separate filing, the DOJ argued that the amended complaint renders moot the motions to dismiss filed by the state, Peltola's campaign, the DSCC and others, citing precedent from the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals. Gleason had given the department until 5 p.m. Alaska Time Thursday to respond to those motions, which seek to have the original complaint thrown out before Election Day on Nov. 3. The judge has not yet ruled on whether the dismissal motions are moot.

The defendants pushed back sharply. Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher and other state election officials filed a motion asking Gleason to expedite consideration of a motion to dismiss the amended complaint, saying the DOJ added a second "equally meritless" count relying on the same legal theory rather than substantively opposing the state's motion. They urged the court not to tolerate what they called "gamesmanship" in the expedited proceedings. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC also filed a new motion to dismiss late Thursday, dismissing the DOJ's new claim and its allegation that they misled the court; they pointed to language in a proposed answer in which they said they lacked knowledge or information sufficient to admit or deny certain allegations.

The case is on a compressed timeline ahead of the Nov. 3 election, and Gleason's next decisions on whether the original dismissal motions are moot and whether to expedite review of the new motions will shape how quickly the dispute is resolved. The state's Public Safety investigation ordered by Dunleavy adds a parallel track that could bear on the allegations about the Sullivan candidacy.
